title: Technical Deep Dive - Guardrails, Performance & Moderation Placement
summary: Redwood SE and AE ran a ~1hr technical deep dive with Atlas HealthTech to discuss how safety filters and moderation affect inference performance. Main points: moderation placement (inline vs async/out-of-band), cost/latency tradeoffs, using smaller fast classifiers, caching moderation results, impact on batching and KV cache, quantization effects on safety models, VPC/on-prem routing and audit requirements. Agreed next steps: run benchmarks with sample prompts, share security docs, propose pilot config and cost estimation.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-10
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maria Lopez (Atlas ML Ops), Darren Kim (Atlas CTO), Priya Nair (Atlas Security)

[00:00] Avery: ok everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to do a technical deep dive on guardrails and how moderation impacts performance across the runtime. Samir and I will run through options, tradeoffs, and some deployment patterns.
[00:18] Maria: thanks, quick context — we're evaluating putting LLM-based summarization and triage into our clinical intake flow. Low latency is critical for triage, but we also must ensure safety and strict audit logs.
[00:35] Darren: right, throughput peaks are important too, we have spikes up to 250 req/s in certain hours.
[00:45] Samir: got it; two big axis today: where to run moderation (inline in the same inference path vs out-of-band/async), and how it interacts with batching, KV cache, and quantized models. We'll also talk VPC/on-prem constraints.
[01:05] Priya: and from security side, we need retention, KMS integration, and that moderation decisions are auditable. Also any PII handling concerns.

--- Moderation placement overview ---
[02:10] Samir: option one is inline synchronous moderation — every prompt goes through a safety model or rule engine before or during generation. Pros: simplest correctness, lowest chance of toxic output reaching client. Cons: adds latency on the critical path.
[02:45] Avery: to quantify, we've measured inline classifier checks adding anywhere from 20ms for a small local classifier up to 200-400ms if you call an external heavier model — depends on where it runs and whether it's GPU-backed.
[03:12] Maria: that matter a lot — our SLO is 300ms p95 for triage. If we add 200-400ms it's a non-starter unless we compensate elsewhere.
[03:25] Samir: exactly — so approaches: 1) run a very small fast classifier (CPU or tiny quantized GPU) inline to catch high-confidence issues, 2) do probabilistic sampling inline + async post-filtering for lower risk cases, 3) do out-of-band full moderation and rollback or shadow-record for audit.

--- Batching and KV cache interactions ---
[05:00] Samir: batching helps throughput but complicates inline moderation: if you batch N requests together, the moderation step's per-request latency can be amortized, but you introduce head-of-line blocking. Also KV cache is sequence-length and session-aware; moderation that depends on generated tokens might invalidate caching assumptions.
[05:35] Maria: can we cache moderation results? Like for repeated prompts or templates?
[05:48] Samir: yes — prefix or prompt-hash caching for moderation decisions works well. If the moderation decision is deterministic and based solely on the prompt content, you can cache the classifier output keyed by a hash of the prompt + context. That reduces overhead particularly for templated flows.
[06:10] Avery: caveat — if moderation uses context including user-specific data or session KV cache, you must include those in the cache key to avoid false negatives. Also cache TTLs and invalidation matters for policy updates.

--- Quantization and safety models ---
[07:00] Samir: smaller, quantized safety models are attractive inline. But quantization can affect classifier calibration — e.g., confidence scores may shift. So we recommend using quantized classifiers only after re-calibrating thresholds and running an A/B on sample distribution.
[07:28] Priya: does Redwood support multiple quantization profiles for safety models separately from the main generator?
[07:35] Samir: yes, you can pin different model variants per route. One pattern: a tiny quantized safety model inline, generator model quantized for cost, and a full-precision safety audit model run async for higher-fidelity checks.

[08:10] Darren: what's the performance hit if we run both inline small classifier and async heavier model?
[08:18] Samir: inline adds maybe 20-80ms for tiny quantized classifiers on CPU / small GPU; async audit doesn't affect latency but will increase cost and complexity (need reconciliation logic if async finds an issue).

--- Placement patterns (detailed) ---
[09:00] Samir: pattern A: Inline-first. Fast classifier inline; if flagged high-confidence, block or escalate. Low/confidence: let it through and mark for async review. Pattern B: Out-of-band-first: generate result, concurrently run safety check; if flagged, issue mitigation (e.g., retract, notify, or replace response) — requires client-side support for retraction or show a holding spinner. Pattern C: Hybrid routing: route traffic by customer tier or route semantics — e.g., 90% through fast path, 10% to strict path with full checks.
[10:05] Maria: hybrid is appealing, we could do strict for clinical categories and fast for administrative text. How do we classify route?
[10:15] Samir: you can do pre-routing with a small intent classifier or rule-based routing; Redwood supports per-route configs and model pinning.

--- Throughput/latency tradeoffs and autoscaling ---
[11:30] Samir: batching + larger GPUs increases throughput but increases tail latency for small single-session requests. For triage you want low p95; recommended: small per-request GPU or CPU path for p95 SLOs, and use autoscale with burst capacity for spikes. Also consider pre-warmed inference workers for known spike windows.
[12:00] Avery: measurement suggestion — run a 95/99 p latency profile for both inline and async placements with synthetic traffic that mirrors your real prompt length distribution. We'll provide a benchmark sheet.

--- KV cache and moderation timing ---
[13:20] Samir: KV cache helps for multi-turn but moderation that inspects generated tokens may cause KV writes to be delayed until after moderation if you want to avoid caching unsafe content. Option: write to KV immediately but mark entries as unapproved and filter when reading from KV for future generations. That keeps performance but means downstream logic must check approval flags.
[14:05] Priya: we need auditability — so marking entries and keeping immutable logs is important. Does Redwood provide audit logs for moderation events?
[14:20] Avery: yes, we can emit per-request audit entries with timestamps and model decisions, stored per retention policy. For Private deployments you can integrate with customer KMS and log sinks.

--- Cost implications ---
[15:00] Samir: running a full-precision classifier on GPU inline for every request is expensive. A common pattern is a two-tier classifier: tiny inline (cheap), heavier async (rarely runs), plus caching. That drives down cost while preserving safety. Also consider offloading high-volume low-risk categories to cheaper models.
[15:28] Maria: any numbers you can share? like per-100k requests cost delta?
[15:35] Avery: rough thumb: tiny CPU classifier + quantized generator can be <50% of heavy GPU generator cost; adding a GPU inline classifier can double costs depending on model sizes. We'll share more detailed numbers in the benchmark spreadsheet.

--- VPC / on-prem constraints ---
[16:20] Samir: in VPC/on-prem, network calls to external moderation services may not be allowed. So inline lightweight classifiers or co-located moderation services are preferred. Redwood's Private mode supports co-located services and audit log sinks.
[16:45] Priya: we also need HSM/KMS integration and SSO for audit access.
[16:52] Avery: we support KMS integrations and RBAC for audit log access; we can map Redwood audit events to your SIEM. We'll include an architecture note.

--- Moderation and batching corner cases ---
[18:10] Samir: corner case: batching with different priority requests — if you mix high- and low-priority users in a batch and moderation fails for one, you might need to drop the whole batch or de-duplicate and re-run, which affects throughput. Best practice: batch by priority or path to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[18:45] Darren: that could complicate autoscaling logic.
[18:50] Samir: yes, simple rule: maintain separate worker pools for strict vs fast paths.

--- Recalibration & metrics ---
[20:00] Samir: when using quantized or smaller safety models, collect false positive/negative rates and adjust thresholds. Use continuous evals: Redwood Optimize can alert on regressions against a prompt set. Also track moderation latency and percent of traffic flagged.
[20:30] Maria: can Redwood's dashboards show per-route moderation rates and token-level cost?
[20:36] Avery: yes — the Console has per-route moderation counts, latency, and token cost breakdowns. We can add custom dashboards for your pilot.

--- Live Q&A and examples ---
[22:00] Maria: example: if a prompt includes PHI and gets tagged high-risk, we want immediate block. Can inline patterns guarantee zero leakage?
[22:12] Samir: inline with strict classifier can keep PHI from being emitted; additional safeguards: response templates, token-level filters, and outbound redaction. For absolute guarantees, you might also do deterministic rule checks on input metadata (e.g., if form field marked PHI, route to strict path).
[23:00] Priya: what about model hallucinations and moderation not catching them?
[23:15] Samir: independent factuality checks are different guardrails; moderation flags toxicity but won't catch hallucinations. For that we recommend grounding sources, citation pipelines, and post-generation verification.

--- Async mitigation patterns ---
[25:00] Samir: async mitigation needs reconciliation: examples — tag response as provisional, run heavy check; if flagged, send a follow-up correction or revoke. UX work required. Another idea: conservative generation templates for high-risk routes to reduce hallucination and toxicity probability.

--- Engineering tradeoffs / metrics to collect ---
[27:30] Samir: collect: p50/p95/p99 latency for generator and moderation separately, moderation false positive/negative rates, percent flagged, cache hit rates for moderation results, cost per 1k requests, and audit log sizes. Those drive configuration.

--- Pilot proposal discussion ---
[30:00] Avery: propose pilot: run 1 week of real traffic in canary mode: 1) route 10% traffic through strict path, 90% through fast path, 2) collect metrics, 3) re-run with different batching/quant settings. We'll run benchmarks and help configure KV cache keys and TTLs.
[30:30] Maria: sounds good; we'll provide sample prompts and traffic profile.

--- Technical nitty-gritty: sample configs ---
[32:00] Samir: suggested config for triage route: inline tiny classifier (quantized 4-bit) on CPU pinned; generator quantized on small GPU with batch size 8 and max latency threshold 300ms. Caching: prompt-hash TTL 10m for templates, user-session KV only for approved content. Audit: stream moderation events to your S3/gcs endpoint with KMS encryption.
[33:15] Darren: if we must run fully on-prem, can we co-locate the audit sink?
[33:22] Avery: yes, for Private deployments we support local sinks and HSM/KMS.

--- Example failure modes ---
[34:30] Samir: 1) stale policy causing false negatives — mitigate with short TTLs or push invalidation hooks; 2) batching mixing priorities — mitigate with separate worker pools; 3) quantized safety drift — mitigate with recalibration and periodic full-precision checks.

--- Costs and quotas ---
[36:00] Samir: we also recommend rate-limiting for moderation-heavy endpoints, and token quotas to avoid runaway cost. Redwood can expose per-route quotas and alerts.

--- Security and compliance specifics ---
[38:00] Priya: audit retention — we need 7 years retention for certain entries — is that supported?
[38:10] Avery: yes, we can configure retention; long-term retention may have cost implications. We can also provide export for legal hold.

--- Closing and recap ---
[58:00] Avery: quick recap: recommended pattern is two-tier moderation (inline small classifier + async high-fidelity), caching of prompt-hash results, careful batching by priority, KV cache flags for approval, quantization with recalibration, and Private deployment patterns for VPC/HSM needs. We'll share configs and benchmark templates.
[58:30] Maria: thanks, that's very helpful.
[58:40] Darren: next steps noted.
[58:50] Priya: we'll send our prompt corpus and network constraints.
[59:05] Avery: action items we'll email and follow up. We'll schedule the pilot run. Thanks everyone.
[59:20] Meeting end.
